facts.title: We ain’t your expectation
facts.description: Travis Yee, an Asian American country singer eloquently sings, “I ain’t your expectation…I may not look or sound like you. Go walk a mile in my shoes. And maybe with a little bit of time. You will see through eyes like mine.” Photo courtesy of Travis Yee. On Sept. 16, 2026, U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon released a Dear Colleague letter, pressuring education leaders and teachers to use the pledge of allegiance. She argued that by reciting these “31 simple words, for a minute a day, students will…take ownership of their citizenship, feel pride in their country.” She co-opted civics learning for the purpose of indoctrination, attempting to weaponize educators and pressure children to show allegiance to a flag which now represents a far right agenda of “making America great again.” Through the whitewashing of history and legislation that strips children of the right to learn about or express their gender identities, the promise of “inalienable” rights remains out of reach for many communities. How can we feel ownership of our home country while our fundamental human rights are being threatened? Why would we feel proud of our country when so many vulnerable people are under siege? Liberty and justice are not experienced equally. title: Mi Jin Kim’s short stories explore the ambiguities of human connection

facts.title: Mi Jin Kim’s short stories explore the ambiguities of human connection
facts.description: Every semester, at least one student asks me why I love books. Without skipping a beat, I reply that books are links between human beings. Centuries ago, someone went through the same thing you did. They wrote about their experience, and that book connects us to them. Through books, we are never truly alone. Mi Jin Kim’s Invitations is one of those books, focusing on the connections between people and what those relationships change within us. Through a series of short stories, the reader follows multiple characters as they attempt to navigate connections – and missed connections – in their own lives. The short stories in Invitations include characters of diverse ages who find themselves in a variety of situations. From a newly-divorced older man to a woman going to the wedding of a childhood friend, to estranged brothers reconnecting from two different continents, the characters aren’t particularly extraordinary. In fact, I would go as far as to say they are the opposite: they are extremely ordinary and familiar. The relatability of a character is usually a cliché, one easily avoided by more in-depth reading, but in the case of Kim’s stories, the relatable moments and reactions of the characters kept me reading. The first story, “Acalpulco,” has cryptic overtones when Hojun, the student of the bitter tutor narrating the story, starts talking about how his father killed his mother. facts.title: Cascadia Art Museum celebrates Zoe Dusanne, who collected and championed Japanese American artists, and linocut artist Shiro Miyazaki
facts.description: Installation view of “Light of Remembrance: The Art of Shirō Miyazaki at the Cascadia Art Museum. Photo by Ana Tanaka. Two prominent Northwest figures are currently memorialized and celebrated in the Cascadia Art Museum: Shiro Miyazaki’s “Light of Remembrance,” and Zoe Dusanne’s “The Art of Seeing,” are both on display until January 3rd, 2027. Shiro Miyazaki: “Light of Remembrance”. Shiro Miyazaki’s exhibit features his extensive body of art that he created during his short and turbulent life. His linocuts and watercolor pieces depict landscapes, stills, and portraits that often convey political commentary or a sort of social message contextualized by the heightened unrest in Japan and the US. Miyazaki (1910–1940), born in Nara Prefecture in Japan, grew up in poverty and, while working as a nomadic farm laborer, used the fruits and vegetables he harvested as painting subjects and then as his meal once he was finished. As recognition for his art grew, his health unfortunately deteriorated and he died of advanced-stage lung cancer at the age of thirty. Throughout the exhibit, many emotions surround Miyazaki’s pieces. One of these pieces, For the Fruits of Our Labor, is a linocut on red paper, circa 1938. Depicting a hand reaching for fruit, the image might be interpreted as a blending of his time as a farm laborer, his tumultuous life, and his declining health manifested in a hand tied down by what looks like smoke, just out of reach of the fruit and light of the sun. facts.title: Japanese Butoh group Sankai Juku to bring their powerful presence in movement and sound to Seattle this month
facts.description: Butoh group Sankai Juku will perform at Seattle’s Moore Theatre on November 17. Photo courtesy. of Seattle Theatre Group. Japanese Butoh dance group Sankai Juku has periodically graced Seattle stages over the past four decades, most recently performing Meguri: Teeming Sea, Tranquil Land in 2019 and Umusuna: Memories Before History in 2015, both at Meany Center for the Performing Arts, and before that, presenting Kagemi — Beyond the Metaphors of Mirrors at the Paramount Theatre in 2006. Now, Sankai Juku returns to the U.S. primarily to tour their newest show TOTEM: Void and Height, but Seattle audiences will instead have the opportunity to see their 2022 composition KoSA (Between Two Mirrors) at the Moore Theatre. Jack McLarnan, STG’s Associate Director of Performing Arts Programs, explains that time and space limitations prevented TOTEM from being performed on The Moore’s stage during this tour, but that STG Presents still wanted to host the troupe. McLarnan believes that Seattle fans of Sankai Juku will experience something unique. “KoSA is lighter on its feet from a production standpoint, but allows us all to experience Sankai Juku’s powerful presence in movement and sound,” he said. “This particular instance is more like a band performing a more stripped down, acoustic set. title: “Nanay” play explores Filipino supernatural horror at Theatre Off Jackson

facts.title: “Nanay” play explores Filipino supernatural horror at Theatre Off Jackson
facts.description: Left: A poster for “Nanay.” Right: playwright Molly Olis Krost. Courtesy image. Two long-standing performing arts organizations, Pork Filled Productions and Theatre Off Jackson, are partnering this autumn to present a world premiere by playwright Molly Olis Krost. Directed by Alyza DelPan-Monley, Krost’s play Nanay centers on adult twin sisters Eve and Angela as they struggle to reconnect following the birth of Eve’s new baby. Throughout the play, Eve and Angela explore their Filipino cultural history and traditions while remembering their nanay, a Tagalog word for mother, who is often viewed as a source of unconditional love as well as the emotional anchor of the family. At the same time, Angela cautiously approaches Eve’s domestic companion Ernesto, who happens to be a Manananggal, a demon that is one variety of many malevolent, shape-shifting creatures in Filipino mythology known as the aswang. By day, Ernesto appears as a typical human, while at night, he transforms into a monster whose hunger is for the hearts and livers of children or unborn fetuses. PFP Executive Director Roger Tang sees Nanay as a good fit for the theatre company in general, and as the final show of the #FilipinoFall initiative in particular. “I think we first saw the show at Seattle Public Theatre’s Distillery series and one of our producers, Alanah Pascual, just fell in love with it,” Tang said. “It’s a funny, yet very deep, heartfelt play about sisterhood, but doesn’t shy away from the...

facts.title: Seattle Community Activist Jenifer Chao Begins as Director of Washington state Commission on Asian Pacific American Affairs
facts.description: Family members of Jenifer Chao, left to right: Youn Choy Chao (father), Mae Seng Chao (mother), Jenifer Chao (with flowers), Christian Chao (son), Jasmine Chao (daughter), Chai Chao (husband). Photo courtesy of Jenifer Chao. Jenifer Chao, newly appointed executive director of the Washington State Commission on Asian Pacific American Affairs (CAPAA), described two childhood memories that shaped her path of work as a community advocate and public servant. “I remember being in kindergarten when someone asked about my identity and I shared that I was Mien,” Chao said. “They responded, ‘What’s that?’ I tried to explain that we are a tribal group originating from China who were displaced to Laos, Vietnam, and Thailand because of war. But they still didn’t understand. At that moment, I felt invisible.”. Chao recalled a second moment in middle school. “One day, the Census folks came to the door,” Chao said. “We had to fill out the form, but Mien wasn’t listed and the closest country our family identified with was Laos. We were from Laos, but we were not Lao. We were Mien. So my mom said, no, we should check the ‘other’ box and specify that we were Mien. My mom told other families to do the same thing. “After I had children of my own, I wanted them to know their identity and feel confident in who they were. title: Bruce Lee Way, a newly named street by Hing Hay Park, honors the late martial arts icon

facts.title: Bruce Lee Way, a newly named street by Hing Hay Park, honors the late martial arts icon
facts.description: Illustration by Ryan Catabay/DRGDRP Creative. Hing Hay Park in the Chinatown International District was buzzing October 16 as a crowd of more than 100 people eagerly awaited the ceremony commemorating Bruce Lee Way, a street newly renamed to honor the late martial arts icon. The new Bruce Lee Way sits on the south side of Hing Hay, between Sixth Avenue South and Maynard Avenue South, in the neighborhood where a young Lee made his mark. That Friday morning ceremony drew scores of community members and city officials to celebrate the street renaming. Many attendees wore Bruce Lee merch. One person dressed up in Lee’s iconic yellow jumpsuit from his unfinished film “Game of Death.”. “Today, Seattle is recognizing an important part of Bruce Lee’s extraordinary journey from a young martial arts instructor in Seattle, to international icon,” said Abe Santos, co-founder of Jun Fan Gung Fu Academy and advocate for the sign. “His influence continues to inspire generations, and now his name will forever be part of the city that helped shape him.”. The ceremony included speeches from Lee’s daughter Shannon Lee, Councilmember Eddie Lin, Deputy Mayor Brian Surratt and Santos, along with a lion dance performed by Seattle Shaolin Kungfu Academy dancers. Every seat was taken, and dozens more attendees stood to watch. Councilmember Eddie Lin speaks on how Bruce Lee inspired him. Photo by Micah Yip. facts.description: Diwali: Lights of India is part of the Seattle Center Festál series. The free event takes place on November 7 from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. at the Seattle Center Armory & Event Hall. Diwali (Festival of Lights) is a major cultural celebration observed throughout India every fall. It symbolizes the victory of light over darkness, good over evil, and knowledge over ignorance. Light is a metaphor for knowledge and consciousness. During Diwali in India, houses and business locations are brightly illuminated with lamps, diyas (oil lamps), and candles. Lakshmi, the Goddess of Wealth, is worshiped for prosperity. Diwali is celebrated with families and friends, wearing new clothes, partaking in family feasts, enjoying delicious sweets, sharing gifts. facts.description: The spending for this year’s election has, so far, stayed on par with past elections, while officials from the agency responsible for oversight say some reporting deadlines can cause issues and announced they cannot enforce a part of the state’s campaign finance laws. This cycle saw about $140 million spent on candidates and issues in Washington. The majority came from political committees, which spent $105 million. “These are so far incomplete numbers,” Deputy Director for the WA Public Disclosure Commission Kim Bradford said. “There will be more after the election because we're in a period right now where there's no reporting of expenditure activity in that last week before the election. Once we get those post-election reports in December, we'll know the totality of what was spent.”. Based on those year-end reports from previous years, this year’s spending was substantially lower than the last election – at about half the spending – but it’s on par with the last midterms which saw about $140 million in spending. title: Mossback's Northwest: The Great Wedding Scandal of 1909

facts.title: Mossback's Northwest: The Great Wedding Scandal of 1909
facts.description: It started with an engagement announcement in early March of 1909. The bride was the daughter of the Archdeacon of the Episcopal Church of California whose family lived in Corte Madera in Marin County at a family home called “Daisy Grange.” What made big news was this: the prospective groom was a young Japanese man who was a member of the archdeacon’s household, and the bride-to-be a young, blue-eyed white woman—“the fair picture of girlish innocence,” one newspaper wrote. What wouldn’t be unusual today was scandalous in California where anti-Asian sentiment was strong. The daughter of an archdeacon marrying a supposed “houseboy” was scandalous on its own, but such interracial marriages were also barred by law in the state. Could their love overcome the marriage ban, social stigma, and an eruption of race hatred? They were about to find out. The groom-to-be was Gunjiro Aoki, a young man said to be in his mid-20s. His fiancé was Helen Gladys Emery, aged 21. Gunjiro was living in the archdeacon’s home to enhance his Christian education. His elder brother was a pastor at an Episcopal mission for Japanese in San Francisco. It was said Gunjiro’s family traced its line to a noble one of ancient samurai. The two fell in love. Helen’s father, John Emery, disapproved, but her mother Sophronia Frances Emery supported the proposed union, creating a family rift. Aoki’s family wasn’t thrilled about the engagement either. title: New Mount Zion Pastor Rev. Johnson Shares Vision Ahead Of Installation Weekend

facts.title: New Mount Zion Pastor Rev. Johnson Shares Vision Ahead Of Installation Weekend
facts.description: Rev. Charles Reginald Johnson Sr. joins the Seattle Medium's Rhythm & News Podcast to discuss his new role as senior pastor of Mount Zion Baptist Church, a 135-year cornerstone of Seattle's Black community. After 17 years leading Cochran Avenue Baptist Church in Los Angeles, Johnson shares his vision ahead of his November 14-15 installation celebration.

title: Youth And Law Forum Marks 36 Years Of Empowering Families Through Legal Education

facts.title: Youth And Law Forum Marks 36 Years Of Empowering Families Through Legal Education
facts.description: Marking its 36th year, the Judge Charles V. Johnson Youth and Law Forum returns Saturday, Nov. 14 in Tukwila, connecting young people and families with judges, attorneys and law enforcement. The free event features workshops, networking with legal professionals, and talks by Erin Jones and Shawn Kemp. Organizer Bobby Alexander explains why attending matters.

title: Lincoln Stuns Franklin 24-20 In Regular Season Finale

facts.title: Lincoln Stuns Franklin 24-20 In Regular Season Finale
facts.description: Lincoln ended a winless season with a stunning 24-20 upset over homecoming host Franklin, capped by quarterback Ben Ward's 61-yard touchdown pass to Zachary Nelson with 2:25 left. The Lynx defense then sealed the win with a goal-line stand, stopping Franklin's final drive on fourth down to secure their first victory.

title: Seattle’s Proposed Fire Department Cuts Expose Stretched Emergency Response System

facts.title: Seattle’s Proposed Fire Department Cuts Expose Stretched Emergency Response System
facts.description: I didn’t understand Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposed budget cuts to the fire department until I found myself giving CPR to a dying man in Magnolia, the kind of peripheral neighborhood of Seattle that is most at risk from her call to cut firefighter hours. It was 5:32 p.m. on that September afternoon when I heard someone collapse onto the dusty trail in Discovery Park, and saw a doctor giving a man CPR while a friend called 911. The question in that moment—When the fuck are the EMTs gonna get here?—is at the heart of the fight over the city budget that will be playing out in Seattle for at least the next few weeks. Wilson’s budget proposes cuts from all city departments, but identifies the biggest cut in the fire department, in the form of a $7 million cut to overtime. It’s part of Wilson’s effort to shrink spending and abandon budget tricks of her predecessors that achieved a legally required “balanced budget” by creating future debts. Wilson won’t raise taxes in the short term, and hasn’t laid out a plan for more progressive revenue. So the pie is not getting bigger, at least in this round of budget wrangling. City Council President Dan Strauss disagrees about how big the pie is, and has released a counterproposal that reverses most of Wilson’s cuts, including increasing fire fighter overtime instead of cutting it. title: King County Regional Homelessness Authority CEO Resigns

facts.title: King County Regional Homelessness Authority CEO Resigns
facts.description: King County Regional Homelessness Authority (KCRHA) CEO Dr. Kelly Kinnison submitted her resignation today after only two years on the job. The announcement comes as the beleaguered agency is in the process of being partially dismantled. In a press release, the KCRHA governing board said Kinnison’s departure reflects the organization’s changes in “mission, purpose, and service scope.” Her resignation will be effective November 16. While Kinnison was not officially pushed out, her resignation is the latest in the ongoing fallout over the KCRHA’s damning forensic evaluation in April that found the agency had lost track of $13 million due to poor internal accounting practices. In response to the audit, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson and King County Executive Girmay Zahilay decided in July to take back administration of about $160 million in homelessness service provider contracts, slashing the KCRHA’s budget by more than two thirds. That remnant was left in charge of coordinating the region’s $67 million grant application to the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). It also keeps several regional functions, such as holding the biennial Point-in-Time census of homelessness in the county. The downscaling has already resulted in 10 layoffs, one voluntary departure and the elimination of six unfilled positions from the agency, PubliCola reported in August. In a prepared statement, Zahilay and Wilson shared polite thank you’s to Kinnison. But Wilson’s quote showed...

facts.title: Black Women Saved Our Empire
facts.description: Let’s think about this for a moment. There is a lot of talk on social media about how Black women voters basically saved America from the very worst of itself. They came out not only in strong numbers, but consistently voted against GOP candidates at the highest rates (between 80 and 90 percent). Now let’s zero in on the results of Texas’s gubernatorial race, which had hardcore MAGA incumbent Greg Abbott facing Gina Hinojosa, a four-term state rep of Texas’ 49th legislative district, which includes Austin. Hinojosa, a Mexican American, defeated Abbott by little over 7 points (Abbot: 45.7 percent; Hinojosa: 52.8 percent). She was the clear winner of this contest. In 2022, however, Abbott defeated Dem superstar Beto O’Rourke by 10 points. What changed between then and now? And one must keep in mind that Hinojosa, a state rep, was pretty obscure when she tossed her name into the race compared to O’Rourke, a US rep. In the words of the Texas Tribune: “People weren’t exactly knocking down Gina Hinojosa’s door to get her to run for governor last year.” But in the months leading to the general election, she became “Abbott’s most viable Democratic challenger yet.” What happened between 2022 and 2026? A surge in Latino voters, and a considerable increase in their support of Democratic candidates. And this surge had a lot to do with Trump’s secret police, ICE. He also congratulated Stuebe’s opponent, Diana Perez, who was winning by a similar margin. Stuebe, who had not formally conceded, did not like this. “You don’t do that for me,” he said, according to the Washington State Standard. More Democratic pickups are possible as votes keep getting counted. The measures vary in severity and scope. Nebraska’s amends the state constitution to ban male students from participating in female sports. Arizona’s adds an athletic institution bathroom ban and extends a trans sports ban to private schools. Colorado’s requires teams from elementary school through college to designate whether they are for male, female, or co-ed participation and require athletes compete based on biological sex. title: Say Cheese!

facts.title: Say Cheese!
facts.description: There is something about this piece of cheese—waterslide transfer print on processed prepared cheese product, to be exact—that’s really doing it for me. Made by Texas-raised, Portland-based artist Ash Stone, it’s on view tonight at RailSpur as part of an exhibition called I Am Love: Rituals in Resistance. The image has been transferred onto the protective plastic sleeve sheathing a glisteny slice of orange cheese: a picture of a trailer, the kind of single- or double-wide you find plentiful in rural Texas. Surrounded by clusters of bright daylilies, an attached staircase-cum-porch leads to the closed front door, where a white-haired woman pauses, her body half-turned toward the viewer. The Mary in Mary’s Garden is Stone’s grandmother, and the raised flowerbeds in the foreground are hers. Another piece of cheese in the show, titled Some Day, is imprinted with words that seem to have been scrawled on a Post-it-sized note: “I love you and am SO proud of you. I’m sorry it’s not the way I had hoped here—maybe it will be some day.”. Ash Stone’s Some Day at RailSpur. Stone’s playfulness is as abundant as the faux cheese on the bottom shelf of a dairy display, and it operates on the same frequency as a Proustian madeleine. The words “say cheese” cling like an aura to the images, forcing smiles. For those of us raised in Texas (Stone included), the image of a trailer might summon a familiar, complicated nostalgia for the containers of our interior world, for home—even if that home...

title: Councilmember Rob Saka Backs Katie Wilson’s RV Ban Veto

facts.title: Councilmember Rob Saka Backs Katie Wilson’s RV Ban Veto
facts.description: At a press conference on Tuesday, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson explained why she issued her first veto against the council’s recently passed RV ban and presented her own alternative executive order. But it was a surprise guest who stole the show: centrist City Councilmember Rob Saka. Saka’s presence signaled his reversal on the controversial RV bill, which he had voted for last month. Together with the three progressives on the council, Saka’s support will be enough to safeguard Wilson’s veto from a potential override. The legislation, sponsored by Councilmember Dan Strauss, would have required RV owners to obtain a special new permit to park their vehicles on city streets for more than two hours. But homelessness advocates and services providers argued the true intent of legislation was to “regulate” (read: banish) RV residents out of city limits altogether. Wilson echoed the concerns over the well-being of homeless vehicle residents, and also said that Strauss’s bill would expose the City to potential lawsuits. It would also cost millions of dollars to set up a new permitting bureaucracy, she said. “It is my responsibility to ensure that our city policies and programs are feasible, are a cost-effective use of public resources, and have a reasonable likelihood of achieving their stated goals,” Wilson said. Wilson did pass Strauss’s four other ordinances to increase outreach funding, set up large vehicle storage lots, and rewrite the City’s definition of junk vehicles. As an...

title: Mi Jin Kim’s short stories explore the ambiguities of human connection

facts.title: Mi Jin Kim’s short stories explore the ambiguities of human connection
facts.description: Every semester, at least one student asks me why I love books. Without skipping a beat, I reply that books are links between human beings. Centuries ago, someone went through the same thing you did. They wrote about their experience, and that book connects us to them. Through books, we are never truly alone. Mi Jin Kim’s Invitations is one of those books, focusing on the connections between people and what those relationships change within us. Through a series of short stories, the reader follows multiple characters as they attempt to navigate connections – and missed connections – in their own lives. The short stories in Invitations include characters of diverse ages who find themselves in a variety of situations. From a newly-divorced older man to a woman going to the wedding of a childhood friend, to estranged brothers reconnecting from two different continents, the characters aren’t particularly extraordinary. In fact, I would go as far as to say they are the opposite: they are extremely ordinary and familiar. The relatability of a character is usually a cliché, one easily avoided by more in-depth reading, but in the case of Kim’s stories, the relatable moments and reactions of the characters kept me reading. The first story, “Acalpulco,” has cryptic overtones when Hojun, the student of the bitter tutor narrating the story, starts talking about how his father killed his mother. facts.description: Installation view of “Light of Remembrance: The Art of Shirō Miyazaki at the Cascadia Art Museum. Photo by Ana Tanaka. Two prominent Northwest figures are currently memorialized and celebrated in the Cascadia Art Museum: Shiro Miyazaki’s “Light of Remembrance,” and Zoe Dusanne’s “The Art of Seeing,” are both on display until January 3rd, 2027. Shiro Miyazaki: “Light of Remembrance”. Shiro Miyazaki’s exhibit features his extensive body of art that he created during his short and turbulent life. His linocuts and watercolor pieces depict landscapes, stills, and portraits that often convey political commentary or a sort of social message contextualized by the heightened unrest in Japan and the US. Miyazaki (1910–1940), born in Nara Prefecture in Japan, grew up in poverty and, while working as a nomadic farm laborer, used the fruits and vegetables he harvested as painting subjects and then as his meal once he was finished. As recognition for his art grew, his health unfortunately deteriorated and he died of advanced-stage lung cancer at the age of thirty. Throughout the exhibit, many emotions surround Miyazaki’s pieces. One of these pieces, For the Fruits of Our Labor, is a linocut on red paper, circa 1938. Depicting a hand reaching for fruit, the image might be interpreted as a blending of his time as a farm laborer, his tumultuous life, and his declining health manifested in a hand tied down by what looks like smoke, just out of reach of the fruit and light of the sun. title: “Nanay” play explores Filipino supernatural horror at Theatre Off Jackson

facts.title: “Nanay” play explores Filipino supernatural horror at Theatre Off Jackson
facts.description: Left: A poster for “Nanay.” Right: playwright Molly Olis Krost. Courtesy image. Two long-standing performing arts organizations, Pork Filled Productions and Theatre Off Jackson, are partnering this autumn to present a world premiere by playwright Molly Olis Krost. Directed by Alyza DelPan-Monley, Krost’s play Nanay centers on adult twin sisters Eve and Angela as they struggle to reconnect following the birth of Eve’s new baby. Throughout the play, Eve and Angela explore their Filipino cultural history and traditions while remembering their nanay, a Tagalog word for mother, who is often viewed as a source of unconditional love as well as the emotional anchor of the family. At the same time, Angela cautiously approaches Eve’s domestic companion Ernesto, who happens to be a Manananggal, a demon that is one variety of many malevolent, shape-shifting creatures in Filipino mythology known as the aswang. By day, Ernesto appears as a typical human, while at night, he transforms into a monster whose hunger is for the hearts and livers of children or unborn fetuses. PFP Executive Director Roger Tang sees Nanay as a good fit for the theatre company in general, and as the final show of the #FilipinoFall initiative in particular. “I think we first saw the show at Seattle Public Theatre’s Distillery series and one of our producers, Alanah Pascual, just fell in love with it,” Tang said. “It’s a funny, yet very deep, heartfelt play about sisterhood, but doesn’t shy away from the...

Jenifer Chao, newly appointed executive director of the Washington State Commission on Asian Pacific American Affairs (CAPAA), described two childhood memories that shaped her path of work as a community advocate and public servant. “I remember being in kindergarten when someone asked about my identity and I shared that I was Mien,” Chao said. “They responded, ‘What’s that?’ I tried to explain that we are a tribal group originating from China who were displaced to Laos, Vietnam, and Thailand because of war. But they still didn’t understand. At that moment, I felt invisible.”. Chao recalled a second moment in middle school. “One day, the Census folks came to the door,” Chao said. “We had to fill out the form, but Mien wasn’t listed and the closest country our family identified with was Laos. The new Bruce Lee Way sits on the south side of Hing Hay, between Sixth Avenue South and Maynard Avenue South, in the neighborhood where a young Lee made his mark. That Friday morning ceremony drew scores of community members and city officials to celebrate the street renaming. Many attendees wore Bruce Lee merch. One person dressed up in Lee’s iconic yellow jumpsuit from his unfinished film “Game of Death.”. “Today, Seattle is recognizing an important part of Bruce Lee’s extraordinary journey from a young martial arts instructor in Seattle, to international icon,” said Abe Santos, co-founder of Jun Fan Gung Fu Academy and advocate for the sign. “His influence continues to inspire generations, and now his name will forever be part of the city that helped shape him.”. title: Seattle’s Proposed Fire Department Cuts Expose Stretched Emergency Response System

facts.title: Seattle’s Proposed Fire Department Cuts Expose Stretched Emergency Response System
facts.description: I didn’t understand Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposed budget cuts to the fire department until I found myself giving CPR to a dying man in Magnolia, the kind of peripheral neighborhood of Seattle that is most at risk from her call to cut firefighter hours. It was 5:32 p.m. on that September afternoon when I heard someone collapse onto the dusty trail in Discovery Park, and saw a doctor giving a man CPR while a friend called 911. The question in that moment—When the fuck are the EMTs gonna get here?—is at the heart of the fight over the city budget that will be playing out in Seattle for at least the next few weeks. Wilson’s budget proposes cuts from all city departments, but identifies the biggest cut in the fire department, in the form of a $7 million cut to overtime. It’s part of Wilson’s effort to shrink spending and abandon budget tricks of her predecessors that achieved a legally required “balanced budget” by creating future debts. Wilson won’t raise taxes in the short term, and hasn’t laid out a plan for more progressive revenue. So the pie is not getting bigger, at least in this round of budget wrangling. City Council President Dan Strauss disagrees about how big the pie is, and has released a counterproposal that reverses most of Wilson’s cuts, including increasing fire fighter overtime instead of cutting it. title: King County Regional Homelessness Authority CEO Resigns

facts.title: King County Regional Homelessness Authority CEO Resigns
facts.description: King County Regional Homelessness Authority (KCRHA) CEO Dr. Kelly Kinnison submitted her resignation today after only two years on the job. The announcement comes as the beleaguered agency is in the process of being partially dismantled. In a press release, the KCRHA governing board said Kinnison’s departure reflects the organization’s changes in “mission, purpose, and service scope.” Her resignation will be effective November 16. While Kinnison was not officially pushed out, her resignation is the latest in the ongoing fallout over the KCRHA’s damning forensic evaluation in April that found the agency had lost track of $13 million due to poor internal accounting practices. In response to the audit, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson and King County Executive Girmay Zahilay decided in July to take back administration of about $160 million in homelessness service provider contracts, slashing the KCRHA’s budget by more than two thirds. That remnant was left in charge of coordinating the region’s $67 million grant application to the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). It also keeps several regional functions, such as holding the biennial Point-in-Time census of homelessness in the county. The downscaling has already resulted in 10 layoffs, one voluntary departure and the elimination of six unfilled positions from the agency, PubliCola reported in August. facts.title: Black Women Saved Our Empire
facts.description: Let’s think about this for a moment. There is a lot of talk on social media about how Black women voters basically saved America from the very worst of itself. They came out not only in strong numbers, but consistently voted against GOP candidates at the highest rates (between 80 and 90 percent). Now let’s zero in on the results of Texas’s gubernatorial race, which had hardcore MAGA incumbent Greg Abbott facing Gina Hinojosa, a four-term state rep of Texas’ 49th legislative district, which includes Austin. Hinojosa, a Mexican American, defeated Abbott by little over 7 points (Abbot: 45.7 percent; Hinojosa: 52.8 percent). She was the clear winner of this contest. In 2022, however, Abbott defeated Dem superstar Beto O’Rourke by 10 points. What changed between then and now? And one must keep in mind that Hinojosa, a state rep, was pretty obscure when she tossed her name into the race compared to O’Rourke, a US rep. In the words of the Texas Tribune: “People weren’t exactly knocking down Gina Hinojosa’s door to get her to run for governor last year.” But in the months leading to the general election, she became “Abbott’s most viable Democratic challenger yet.” What happened between 2022 and 2026? title: Say Cheese!

facts.title: Say Cheese!
facts.description: There is something about this piece of cheese—waterslide transfer print on processed prepared cheese product, to be exact—that’s really doing it for me. Made by Texas-raised, Portland-based artist Ash Stone, it’s on view tonight at RailSpur as part of an exhibition called I Am Love: Rituals in Resistance. The image has been transferred onto the protective plastic sleeve sheathing a glisteny slice of orange cheese: a picture of a trailer, the kind of single- or double-wide you find plentiful in rural Texas. Surrounded by clusters of bright daylilies, an attached staircase-cum-porch leads to the closed front door, where a white-haired woman pauses, her body half-turned toward the viewer. The Mary in Mary’s Garden is Stone’s grandmother, and the raised flowerbeds in the foreground are hers. Another piece of cheese in the show, titled Some Day, is imprinted with words that seem to have been scrawled on a Post-it-sized note: “I love you and am SO proud of you. I’m sorry it’s not the way I had hoped here—maybe it will be some day.”. Ash Stone’s Some Day at RailSpur. Stone’s playfulness is as abundant as the faux cheese on the bottom shelf of a dairy display, and it operates on the same frequency as a Proustian madeleine. The words “say cheese” cling like an aura to the images, forcing smiles. For those of us raised in Texas (Stone included), the image of a trailer might summon a familiar, complicated nostalgia for the containers of our interior world, for home—even if that home...

title: Councilmember Rob Saka Backs Katie Wilson’s RV Ban Veto

facts.title: Councilmember Rob Saka Backs Katie Wilson’s RV Ban Veto
facts.description: At a press conference on Tuesday, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson explained why she issued her first veto against the council’s recently passed RV ban and presented her own alternative executive order. But it was a surprise guest who stole the show: centrist City Councilmember Rob Saka. Saka’s presence signaled his reversal on the controversial RV bill, which he had voted for last month. Together with the three progressives on the council, Saka’s support will be enough to safeguard Wilson’s veto from a potential override. The legislation, sponsored by Councilmember Dan Strauss, would have required RV owners to obtain a special new permit to park their vehicles on city streets for more than two hours. But homelessness advocates and services providers argued the true intent of legislation was to “regulate” (read: banish) RV residents out of city limits altogether. Wilson echoed the concerns over the well-being of homeless vehicle residents, and also said that Strauss’s bill would expose the City to potential lawsuits. It would also cost millions of dollars to set up a new permitting bureaucracy, she said. “It is my responsibility to ensure that our city policies and programs are feasible, are a cost-effective use of public resources, and have a reasonable likelihood of achieving their stated goals,” Wilson said. facts.description: The spending for this year’s election has, so far, stayed on par with past elections, while officials from the agency responsible for oversight say some reporting deadlines can cause issues and announced they cannot enforce a part of the state’s campaign finance laws. This cycle saw about $140 million spent on candidates and issues in Washington. The majority came from political committees, which spent $105 million. “These are so far incomplete numbers,” Deputy Director for the WA Public Disclosure Commission Kim Bradford said. “There will be more after the election because we're in a period right now where there's no reporting of expenditure activity in that last week before the election. Once we get those post-election reports in December, we'll know the totality of what was spent.”. Based on those year-end reports from previous years, this year’s spending was substantially lower than the last election – at about half the spending – but it’s on par with the last midterms which saw about $140 million in spending. The agency gets those numbers from the campaigns themselves in reports required before and after the election, including reports 21 days and 7 days from the election, but officials say those reporting deadlines cause issues. “For a number of years the commission has been discussing what we've come to call “the dark period,” Bradford said. “That is the period between September 1st and about middle of October. title: Mossback's Northwest: The Great Wedding Scandal of 1909

facts.title: Mossback's Northwest: The Great Wedding Scandal of 1909
facts.description: It started with an engagement announcement in early March of 1909. The bride was the daughter of the Archdeacon of the Episcopal Church of California whose family lived in Corte Madera in Marin County at a family home called “Daisy Grange.” What made big news was this: the prospective groom was a young Japanese man who was a member of the archdeacon’s household, and the bride-to-be a young, blue-eyed white woman—“the fair picture of girlish innocence,” one newspaper wrote. What wouldn’t be unusual today was scandalous in California where anti-Asian sentiment was strong. The daughter of an archdeacon marrying a supposed “houseboy” was scandalous on its own, but such interracial marriages were also barred by law in the state. Could their love overcome the marriage ban, social stigma, and an eruption of race hatred? They were about to find out. The groom-to-be was Gunjiro Aoki, a young man said to be in his mid-20s. His fiancé was Helen Gladys Emery, aged 21. Gunjiro was living in the archdeacon’s home to enhance his Christian education. His elder brother was a pastor at an Episcopal mission for Japanese in San Francisco. It was said Gunjiro’s family traced its line to a noble one of ancient samurai. The two fell in love. Helen’s father, John Emery, disapproved, but her mother Sophronia Frances Emery supported the proposed union, creating a family rift. Aoki’s family wasn’t thrilled about the engagement either. title: Mi Jin Kim’s short stories explore the ambiguities of human connection

facts.title: Mi Jin Kim’s short stories explore the ambiguities of human connection
facts.description: Every semester, at least one student asks me why I love books. Without skipping a beat, I reply that books are links between human beings. Centuries ago, someone went through the same thing you did. They wrote about their experience, and that book connects us to them. Through books, we are never truly alone. Mi Jin Kim’s Invitations is one of those books, focusing on the connections between people and what those relationships change within us. Through a series of short stories, the reader follows multiple characters as they attempt to navigate connections – and missed connections – in their own lives. The short stories in Invitations include characters of diverse ages who find themselves in a variety of situations. From a newly-divorced older man to a woman going to the wedding of a childhood friend, to estranged brothers reconnecting from two different continents, the characters aren’t particularly extraordinary. In fact, I would go as far as to say they are the opposite: they are extremely ordinary and familiar. The relatability of a character is usually a cliché, one easily avoided by more in-depth reading, but in the case of Kim’s stories, the relatable moments and reactions of the characters kept me reading. The first story, “Acalpulco,” has cryptic overtones when Hojun, the student of the bitter tutor narrating the story, starts talking about how his father killed his mother. title: Cascadia Art Museum celebrates Zoe Dusanne, who collected and championed Japanese American artists, and linocut artist Shiro Miyazaki

facts.title: Cascadia Art Museum celebrates Zoe Dusanne, who collected and championed Japanese American artists, and linocut artist Shiro Miyazaki
facts.description: Installation view of “Light of Remembrance: The Art of Shirō Miyazaki at the Cascadia Art Museum. Photo by Ana Tanaka. Two prominent Northwest figures are currently memorialized and celebrated in the Cascadia Art Museum: Shiro Miyazaki’s “Light of Remembrance,” and Zoe Dusanne’s “The Art of Seeing,” are both on display until January 3rd, 2027. Shiro Miyazaki: “Light of Remembrance”. Shiro Miyazaki’s exhibit features his extensive body of art that he created during his short and turbulent life. His linocuts and watercolor pieces depict landscapes, stills, and portraits that often convey political commentary or a sort of social message contextualized by the heightened unrest in Japan and the US. Miyazaki (1910–1940), born in Nara Prefecture in Japan, grew up in poverty and, while working as a nomadic farm laborer, used the fruits and vegetables he harvested as painting subjects and then as his meal once he was finished. As recognition for his art grew, his health unfortunately deteriorated and he died of advanced-stage lung cancer at the age of thirty. Throughout the exhibit, many emotions surround Miyazaki’s pieces. One of these pieces, For the Fruits of Our Labor, is a linocut on red paper, circa 1938. Depicting a hand reaching for fruit, the image might be interpreted as a blending of his time as a farm laborer, his tumultuous life, and his declining health manifested in a hand tied down by what looks like smoke, just out of reach of the fruit and light of the sun. title: Japanese Butoh group Sankai Juku to bring their powerful presence in movement and sound to Seattle this month

facts.title: Japanese Butoh group Sankai Juku to bring their powerful presence in movement and sound to Seattle this month
facts.description: Butoh group Sankai Juku will perform at Seattle’s Moore Theatre on November 17. Photo courtesy. of Seattle Theatre Group. Japanese Butoh dance group Sankai Juku has periodically graced Seattle stages over the past four decades, most recently performing Meguri: Teeming Sea, Tranquil Land in 2019 and Umusuna: Memories Before History in 2015, both at Meany Center for the Performing Arts, and before that, presenting Kagemi — Beyond the Metaphors of Mirrors at the Paramount Theatre in 2006. Now, Sankai Juku returns to the U.S. primarily to tour their newest show TOTEM: Void and Height, but Seattle audiences will instead have the opportunity to see their 2022 composition KoSA (Between Two Mirrors) at the Moore Theatre. Jack McLarnan, STG’s Associate Director of Performing Arts Programs, explains that time and space limitations prevented TOTEM from being performed on The Moore’s stage during this tour, but that STG Presents still wanted to host the troupe. McLarnan believes that Seattle fans of Sankai Juku will experience something unique. “KoSA is lighter on its feet from a production standpoint, but allows us all to experience Sankai Juku’s powerful presence in movement and sound,” he said. “This particular instance is more like a band performing a more stripped down, acoustic set. title: “Nanay” play explores Filipino supernatural horror at Theatre Off Jackson

facts.title: “Nanay” play explores Filipino supernatural horror at Theatre Off Jackson
facts.description: Left: A poster for “Nanay.” Right: playwright Molly Olis Krost. Courtesy image. Two long-standing performing arts organizations, Pork Filled Productions and Theatre Off Jackson, are partnering this autumn to present a world premiere by playwright Molly Olis Krost. Directed by Alyza DelPan-Monley, Krost’s play Nanay centers on adult twin sisters Eve and Angela as they struggle to reconnect following the birth of Eve’s new baby. Throughout the play, Eve and Angela explore their Filipino cultural history and traditions while remembering their nanay, a Tagalog word for mother, who is often viewed as a source of unconditional love as well as the emotional anchor of the family. At the same time, Angela cautiously approaches Eve’s domestic companion Ernesto, who happens to be a Manananggal, a demon that is one variety of many malevolent, shape-shifting creatures in Filipino mythology known as the aswang. By day, Ernesto appears as a typical human, while at night, he transforms into a monster whose hunger is for the hearts and livers of children or unborn fetuses. facts.description: Illustration by Ryan Catabay/DRGDRP Creative. Hing Hay Park in the Chinatown International District was buzzing October 16 as a crowd of more than 100 people eagerly awaited the ceremony commemorating Bruce Lee Way, a street newly renamed to honor the late martial arts icon. The new Bruce Lee Way sits on the south side of Hing Hay, between Sixth Avenue South and Maynard Avenue South, in the neighborhood where a young Lee made his mark. That Friday morning ceremony drew scores of community members and city officials to celebrate the street renaming. Many attendees wore Bruce Lee merch. One person dressed up in Lee’s iconic yellow jumpsuit from his unfinished film “Game of Death.”. “Today, Seattle is recognizing an important part of Bruce Lee’s extraordinary journey from a young martial arts instructor in Seattle, to international icon,” said Abe Santos, co-founder of Jun Fan Gung Fu Academy and advocate for the sign. “His influence continues to inspire generations, and now his name will forever be part of the city that helped shape him.”. facts.description: I didn’t understand Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposed budget cuts to the fire department until I found myself giving CPR to a dying man in Magnolia, the kind of peripheral neighborhood of Seattle that is most at risk from her call to cut firefighter hours. It was 5:32 p.m. on that September afternoon when I heard someone collapse onto the dusty trail in Discovery Park, and saw a doctor giving a man CPR while a friend called 911. The question in that moment—When the fuck are the EMTs gonna get here?—is at the heart of the fight over the city budget that will be playing out in Seattle for at least the next few weeks. Wilson’s budget proposes cuts from all city departments, but identifies the biggest cut in the fire department, in the form of a $7 million cut to overtime. It’s part of Wilson’s effort to shrink spending and abandon budget tricks of her predecessors that achieved a legally required “balanced budget” by creating future debts. Wilson won’t raise taxes in the short term, and hasn’t laid out a plan for more progressive revenue. So the pie is not getting bigger, at least in this round of budget wrangling. City Council President Dan Strauss disagrees about how big the pie is, and has released a counterproposal that reverses most of Wilson’s cuts, including increasing fire fighter overtime instead of cutting it. facts.title: King County Regional Homelessness Authority CEO Resigns
facts.description: King County Regional Homelessness Authority (KCRHA) CEO Dr. Kelly Kinnison submitted her resignation today after only two years on the job. The announcement comes as the beleaguered agency is in the process of being partially dismantled. In a press release, the KCRHA governing board said Kinnison’s departure reflects the organization’s changes in “mission, purpose, and service scope.” Her resignation will be effective November 16. While Kinnison was not officially pushed out, her resignation is the latest in the ongoing fallout over the KCRHA’s damning forensic evaluation in April that found the agency had lost track of $13 million due to poor internal accounting practices. In response to the audit, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson and King County Executive Girmay Zahilay decided in July to take back administration of about $160 million in homelessness service provider contracts, slashing the KCRHA’s budget by more than two thirds. That remnant was left in charge of coordinating the region’s $67 million grant application to the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). It also keeps several regional functions, such as holding the biennial Point-in-Time census of homelessness in the county. The downscaling has already resulted in 10 layoffs, one voluntary departure and the elimination of six unfilled positions from the agency, PubliCola reported in August. title: Say Cheese!

facts.title: Say Cheese!
facts.description: There is something about this piece of cheese—waterslide transfer print on processed prepared cheese product, to be exact—that’s really doing it for me. Made by Texas-raised, Portland-based artist Ash Stone, it’s on view tonight at RailSpur as part of an exhibition called I Am Love: Rituals in Resistance. The image has been transferred onto the protective plastic sleeve sheathing a glisteny slice of orange cheese: a picture of a trailer, the kind of single- or double-wide you find plentiful in rural Texas. Surrounded by clusters of bright daylilies, an attached staircase-cum-porch leads to the closed front door, where a white-haired woman pauses, her body half-turned toward the viewer. The Mary in Mary’s Garden is Stone’s grandmother, and the raised flowerbeds in the foreground are hers. Another piece of cheese in the show, titled Some Day, is imprinted with words that seem to have been scrawled on a Post-it-sized note: “I love you and am SO proud of you. I’m sorry it’s not the way I had hoped here—maybe it will be some day.”. Ash Stone’s Some Day at RailSpur. Stone’s playfulness is as abundant as the faux cheese on the bottom shelf of a dairy display, and it operates on the same frequency as a Proustian madeleine. The words “say cheese” cling like an aura to the images, forcing smiles. For those of us raised in Texas (Stone included), the image of a trailer might summon a familiar, complicated nostalgia for the containers of our interior world, for home—even if that home...

title: Councilmember Rob Saka Backs Katie Wilson’s RV Ban Veto

facts.title: Councilmember Rob Saka Backs Katie Wilson’s RV Ban Veto
facts.description: At a press conference on Tuesday, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson explained why she issued her first veto against the council’s recently passed RV ban and presented her own alternative executive order. But it was a surprise guest who stole the show: centrist City Councilmember Rob Saka. Saka’s presence signaled his reversal on the controversial RV bill, which he had voted for last month. Together with the three progressives on the council, Saka’s support will be enough to safeguard Wilson’s veto from a potential override. The legislation, sponsored by Councilmember Dan Strauss, would have required RV owners to obtain a special new permit to park their vehicles on city streets for more than two hours. But homelessness advocates and services providers argued the true intent of legislation was to “regulate” (read: banish) RV residents out of city limits altogether. Wilson echoed the concerns over the well-being of homeless vehicle residents, and also said that Strauss’s bill would expose the City to potential lawsuits. It would also cost millions of dollars to set up a new permitting bureaucracy, she said. “It is my responsibility to ensure that our city policies and programs are feasible, are a cost-effective use of public resources, and have a reasonable likelihood of achieving their stated goals,” Wilson said. facts.title: WA campaign spending rules leave “dark period” close to elections
facts.description: The spending for this year’s election has, so far, stayed on par with past elections, while officials from the agency responsible for oversight say some reporting deadlines can cause issues and announced they cannot enforce a part of the state’s campaign finance laws. This cycle saw about $140 million spent on candidates and issues in Washington. The majority came from political committees, which spent $105 million. “These are so far incomplete numbers,” Deputy Director for the WA Public Disclosure Commission Kim Bradford said. “There will be more after the election because we're in a period right now where there's no reporting of expenditure activity in that last week before the election. Once we get those post-election reports in December, we'll know the totality of what was spent.”. Based on those year-end reports from previous years, this year’s spending was substantially lower than the last election – at about half the spending – but it’s on par with the last midterms which saw about $140 million in spending. The agency gets those numbers from the campaigns themselves in reports required before and after the election, including reports 21 days and 7 days from the election, but officials say those reporting deadlines cause issues. “For a number of years the commission has been discussing what we've come to call “the dark period,” Bradford said. “That is the period between September 1st and about middle of October. title: Mossback's Northwest: The Great Wedding Scandal of 1909

facts.title: Mossback's Northwest: The Great Wedding Scandal of 1909
facts.description: It started with an engagement announcement in early March of 1909. The bride was the daughter of the Archdeacon of the Episcopal Church of California whose family lived in Corte Madera in Marin County at a family home called “Daisy Grange.” What made big news was this: the prospective groom was a young Japanese man who was a member of the archdeacon’s household, and the bride-to-be a young, blue-eyed white woman—“the fair picture of girlish innocence,” one newspaper wrote. What wouldn’t be unusual today was scandalous in California where anti-Asian sentiment was strong. The daughter of an archdeacon marrying a supposed “houseboy” was scandalous on its own, but such interracial marriages were also barred by law in the state. Could their love overcome the marriage ban, social stigma, and an eruption of race hatred? They were about to find out. The groom-to-be was Gunjiro Aoki, a young man said to be in his mid-20s. His fiancé was Helen Gladys Emery, aged 21. Gunjiro was living in the archdeacon’s home to enhance his Christian education. His elder brother was a pastor at an Episcopal mission for Japanese in San Francisco. It was said Gunjiro’s family traced its line to a noble one of ancient samurai. The two fell in love. Helen’s father, John Emery, disapproved, but her mother Sophronia Frances Emery supported the proposed union, creating a family rift. Aoki’s family wasn’t thrilled about the engagement either. facts.title: 3D Printer Orientation: The Basics @ NESTL
facts.venue: NE Seattle Tool Library, 10228 Fischer Place Northeast, Seattle, WA, 98125, United States
facts.description: Learn how to use our 3D printers. 3D Printer Orientation is necessary to use our in-house Prusa MK3S+ 3D printers. Learn how to find, prepare, and print 3D models on our Prusa MK3S+ 3D printers! No previous knowledge is required. This class will cover where to source 3D models online, how to slice files using Prusa Slicer, and how to operate the machine. You are encouraged to bring your own laptop to the class and download Prusa Slicer by clicking here, but it is not required. This class will not include a 3D modeling aspect. If you are interested in learning 3D modeling, check out our other class—CAD for 3D Printing. Please note that CAD for 3D Printing class is NOT a 3D printer orientation class and will not cover how to use our in-house 3D printers. These classes will not have any content overlap. If you are interested in taking both, you can take them in either order. Taking the 3D Printer Orientation is required to use our in-house printers. You must also be a member of NE Seattle Tool Library or Shoreline Tool Library to take this class. Become a member here! While this instance is at the NE Seattle Tool Library, we also have 3D Printer Orientations at the Shoreline Tool Library, and completing one at either location gives members access to all of our tool library 3D printers. You may view our full list of upcoming 3D Printer Orientations here. Our sliding scale for classes helps to reduce barriers for participation while retaining sufficient income for Seattle...

facts.title: Learn How to Knit (Optional 2-Part Class) @ RCLC
facts.venue: 12558 Lake City Way NE, 12558 Lake City Way Northeast, Seattle, WA, 98125, United States
facts.description: Learn the basics of knitting so you can start you first project and get hands-on support in the second session. Some materials required. This two-session class will give you the skills and confidence to start your first knitting project. The first session (11/7) will cover the basic steps of knitting. This includes the tools you need, casting on stitches, making both knit and purl stitches, and binding off stitches. The first session will include a discussion of beginner projects, how to read a pattern, and how to pick out materials for a project. The focus of the first session is on practicing the skills rather than starting a project. The second session (11/14) will be optional and structured more like office hours. Students can come and work on projects together, and the instructor will be on hand to provide support. This could include working on an in-progress project, getting help applying the skills from the first class to a specific project, or picking out the pattern for a first project. Students need to bring: Students need to bring: Two double-pointed needles size 7-9 and worsted-weight (medium-thick) yarn. Note that if students already have other needle sizes and yarn weights, they will work and buying more is not necessary. Below are the dates for each part of the class. facts.title: Learn the Basics of Needle Felting and Make a Holiday Ornament @ STL
facts.venue: Shoreline Tool Library, 16610 Aurora Avenue North, Shoreline, WA, 98133, United States
facts.description: Learn about the basic supplies and tools of needle felting (AKA roving), while creating a felted acorn to decorate your home this winter. In this class, you will learn the basics of needle felting with wool. This will include an overview of setup, materials, and tools, along with some tips and tricks to make getting started easier. Students will quickly get into trying out the needle felting by making a simple felted acorn, a lovely little holiday ornament. Hand dexterity is the primary mobility consideration, due the requirement of repetitive and precise movements. Please be aware that in working with needles, you may poke yourself in the process of learning. If you use reading glasses, please bring those along! This class is for absolute beginners, no experience necessary. Although materials will be provided, these are the materials we will be using if you’d like to bring your own: 1 oz of off-white or cream-colored felting wool (looks best with the acorn top, but can be any color). Two 38, 40 or 42 gauge felting needles. One foam or wool felting pad at least 5″x5″. Check out these places for supplies: Wool Friends. Seattle ReCreative. Seattle Yarn. About the instructor, Kristina Krause: Kristina has years of experience with needle felting, among other crafts, and has successfully taught this popular class many times for us. facts.title: Machine Sewing 101
facts.venue: Shoreline Tool Library, 16610 Aurora Avenue North, Shoreline, WA, 98133, United States
facts.description: Learn sewing machine basics, stitches, threading, tension, best practices, and more! Leave with a sampler, PDF guide and confidence. Students will leave this class with the foundation for utilizing a standard home sewing machine. Whether you’re a complete beginner or looking for a refresher, this workshop will teach you all the ins and outs of a standard home sewing machine. We’ll use the Shoreline Tool Library’s sewing machines to explore questions like…. How do sewing machines work? When should I use each stitch? What’s a bobbin and how do I thread it? Why do all the parts have funny names? What’s the deal with the tension? Is this thing I heard about sewing a rule or a guideline? How soon can I make my dream project? And so much more! You’ll come away with an understanding of machine sewing best practices, a stitch sampler, a PDF with all the information we cover in class, and the confidence to start tackling some projects. About the instructor, Ruth Tomandl and Joslyn Slaughter: Ruth has been machine sewing for 25 years and enjoy mending, quilting, and making useful things. Joslyn learned to sew in Home Ec (economics) class in high school back when they taught such a thing.. the 1970s! She’s stock piled more fabric than she’ll ever be able to use; fabric stores are one of her happy places! facts.description: It's time to chat and craft together. Bring your textiles or craft supplies (or use our sewing supplies), and get to know your community! Got a collection of hole-filled socks you can’t get rid of? Have you been meaning to set aside time for your latest alteration, but need some motivation? Come mend with us! Our Community Threads mending and sewing circle is a monthly event for anyone to work on their textile projects. Any textile craft is welcome! Honestly, any craft is welcome, but we will only be providing sewing supplies (at least at first). There will be sewing machines, fabric, thread and community, as well as hot tea. This will not be a class format, while there will be experienced menders present to offer advice and counsel, this is intended as a co-working space. Can’t make it to this one? We plan to host it on the second weekend of each month: The second Saturday at the Shoreline Tool Library and the second Sunday at Reuse Commons Lake City (new location!)! As it grows, we may change it to a different day, but we’ll let you know on social media. ACCESSIBILITY: Much of the venue is wheelchair accessible. facts.description: John, the owner of Renaissance Tree Care, will teach you the basics of how to take care of a range of fruit trees. Some materials required. John will facilitate and lead a discussion about basic fruit tree biology and fruit tree structure, and why we prune or don’t prune based on goals and the species of tree or shrub. He has owned and operated Renaissance Tree Care for over 35 years and has taught his employees everything they need to know for tree care. facts.description: Give a scraggly, overgrown plant a fresh start or learn how to propagate it into new plants! You can bring your own or use one of ours. This hands-on class covers the basics of plant propagation, including stem and leaf cuttings, division, and water propagation. You’ll learn where and how to make cuts, which methods work best for different plants, and how propagation can transform tired, leggy plants into beautiful new ones. You can bring your own plant from home, or you can use one of ours! About the instructor, Jay Galligher: Jay is a native Washingtonian, a Master Gardener–trained plant educator, and the founder of plantbaby, Seattle’s sustainable plant marketplace. Through plantbaby, he connects plant lovers with locally grown houseplants while promoting peat-free soil, reclaimed materials, and environmentally responsible growing practices. facts.description: Come join us for our monthly Volunteer Orientation, where you'll gain new skills, learn about our organization, and meet other volunteers! This is a great opportunity to learn more about how you can get involved with the community and help out at the NE Seattle Tool Library. Whether you’re a seasoned volunteer, you haven’t been back in a while, or you’re brand new, everyone is welcome! We’ll cover everything you need to know about Seattle REconomy’s history and mission, and our community will welcome you to become a part of it. We’ll also go over all of the different ways to volunteer, from Front Desk to Bike Shack, beautification to steering committees, inventory, teaching, fixing tools, outreach, and more! If you’d like to take your first step to supporting this economy of reuse, sign up below and we’ll see you there! If you want to study ahead, check out seattlereconomy.org/volunteer, to find details about all our current opportunities to get involved. Perks of being a Seattle REconomy tool library volunteer? Free tool library membership when you volunteer 1 shift (or 3 hours) per month. Access to our Ridwell bin. Free Seattle REconomy class if you volunteer 3 shifts (or 9 hours) in one month (learn more about our classes on seattlereconomy.org/classes-events). Warm fuzzy feelings! facts.description: It's time to chat and craft together. Bring your textiles or craft supplies (or use our sewing supplies), and get to know your community! facts.title: Learn to Sew Wrapping Cloths or Cloth Napkins @ STL
facts.venue: Shoreline Tool Library, 16610 Aurora Avenue North, Shoreline, WA, 98133, United States
facts.description: Turn squares of fabric into beautifully finished cloth napkins or gift-wrapping cloths. Some materials & basic sewing skills required. Perfect for the holidays, either for you to use or to give as a gift. Learn how to transform simple squares of fabric into beautifully finished cloth napkins or gift wrapping cloths with even hems and mitered corners. While this is a beginner class, the instructor requires that students can already sew a straight line, backstitch, and understand basic sewing machine terminology. Materials Required: Prior to class, each student should decide if they plan to make either wrapping cloths or cloth napkins. There are general materials requirements, along with ones specific to what you plan on creating. All students must bring: NON-STRETCH woven fabric, measuring at least 18×18” inches per napkin or 16×16” per wrap, washed and dried. (Example: 1 ¼ yard of continuous fabric will make four 18×18” hemmed cloths. A size L women’s boxy top will probably make two.). All-purpose thread to match the color of your fabric (optional). Hot tip: Thrift shops and Seattle ReCreative are great places to look for fabrics! If you plan to make gift wrapping cloths: Lightweight fabric of any composition (cotton/ linen/ hemp will be easiest to work with). Sizes between 16×16” and 44×44” recommended. If you plan to make napkins: Midweight cotton, linen, and hemp recommended (synthetic and synthetic blends NOT recommended). Sizes between 21”x21” and 24×24” recommended...

facts.venue: Reuse Commons Lake City, 12558 Lake City Way NE, Seattle, WA, 98125, United States
facts.description: If you have a working sewing machine that you're not sure how to operate, we'll teach you how to use it and answer all of your questions! Do you have a sewing machine but are not sure how to use it or what it can do? Bring your own machine to this class, and our instructors will guide you through using it. We can cover plugging everything in, threading, basic stitches, basic tension adjustments, your bobbin type, winding a bobbin, needles, sewing feet you have or can buy, basic maintenance, and cleaning. We will not be able to service your machine, and you must confirm that it is operational and can form a stitch. If you are not sure, bring your machine to a sewing service shop, and they can confirm and/or provide a service. City Sew & Vac usually has the fastest turnaround of a week or less. Please come with the following: A working sewing machine (including a working power cord, foot pedal, presser foot, and bobbin to match your machine). The machine’s manual (original or printed). 2 new needles for your machine. Quality thread (recommended: Gutterman, Aurofil, Mettler, orMadeira). About the instructors, Karen, Susan Gregory, Jen Yasis, and Ruth Tomandl: Karen, Susan, Jen, and Ruth have many decades of combined experience with operating, cleaning, and maintaining a wide variety of sewing machine types. facts.description: Let’s discuss "The Heaven & Earth Grocery Store" by James McBride. Bring surplus food and/or household items you would like to give away! Join us for the NE Seattle Tool Library’s book club! We’ll be reading The Heaven & Earth Grocery Store” by James McBride. Everyone is invited to bring food or household items they have a surplus of and would like to give away. Bought too much rice for your ambitious paella project? Bring it! Have a gently used candle that just wasn’t your scent? Bring it! All are welcome at book club (even if you haven’t read the book)! It’s all about community, connecting with like-minded people, and sharing a love of books. We hope to see you there for some discussion and community building. If it is nice out, we’ll be hosting this one outside! While we’ll always have tea available, please feel free to bring anything to share. Looking for a copy? Check out Seattle Public Libraries and King County Libraries! We also suggest thriftbooks.com and betterworldbooks.com for ordering used books. Our group agreements are as follows: Respect! Respect people’s opinions, pronouns, bodies, spaces, and time. Keep it flowing. While we wish we could be at book club all night, we only have an hour and a half. Please be mindful of leaving room for everyone to speak. Lead with curiosity. This is a place for expanding our ideas of whats possible! If you haven’t read the book, you are still welcome! title: Dahl Field Restroom Renovation Schedule Update

facts.title: Dahl Field Restroom Renovation Schedule Update
facts.description: The restroom facility at Dahl Field has been closed since it sustained damage from a fire. The timeline of its repair has been a regular question for members in our community. Seattle Parks updated their Dahl Field Restroom Renovation website on October 20th with their latest schedule. Seattle Parks now plans on having the contractor under contract by early 2027 with the goal of construction beginning winter/spring 2027 and wrapping up in the summer of 2027. Seattle Parks appears on-track with this schedule as the city currently has the procurement documents published with the bid for construction to close on November 4th. After that, Seattle Parks will review responses from prospective bidders and award the project to a contractor. The City noted to expect reduced parking at Dahl Field during construction.

facts.description: Watch out! Ghosts, goblins, princesses, and enderman will be over taking 35th Ave NE and patronizing the wonderful businesses for Wedgwood’s annual trick or treat through the 35th Ave NE business district! This is a family-friendly event that the Wedgwood Communit Council organizes each year. We are still looking for another 1-2 volunteers to help kids and their adults cross safely at NE 85th Street and NE 75th Street. If you’re able to help, please email us at admin@wedgwoodcc.org.

title: Land use event Monday, November 9th

facts.title: Land use event Monday, November 9th
facts.description: Community council board member Rachel Nathanson wanted to let everyone know about a land use event she is part of that’s happening soon, here it is in her words: Seattle Residents for Thoughtful Growth (SRTG) is hosting an educational forum on land use actions in Seattle on Monday, November 9th at the Maple Leaf Lutheran Church, from 7-8:30PM. Our mission is to propose growth strategies for Seattle that result in housing attainable to middle income households, protect the environment and support livable neighborhoods. We work with over 30 Seattle neighborhoods (including Wedgwood) advocating for legislation to encourage smaller, more affordable market-rate housing that working class and middle income families can afford. The One Seattle Plan (current zoning changes planned for our city) is legislating “upzoning” in order to provide needed housing. We have evaluated various options to provide true middle housing – smaller units with shared walls that are more affordable. Whatever your opinion is about growing our city, we want to provide information on what the city plans are so that you are informed, and have a discussion on what the best options are for expanding housing. SRTG hosted a similar forum last June to standing room only. We want to bring this information to you and hope you’ll join us on November 9th. Maple Leaf Lutheran Church, 10005 32nd Ave NE. Find out more and RSVP here. It’s free.
